Name: situational_awareness_probe
Title: Are You Being Watched? Probing for Evaluation-Awareness in LLMs
Short Hypothesis: LLMs internally represent whether they are being evaluated/tested versus deployed, this representation is linearly decodable, and its activation correlates with behavioral shifts (e.g., higher safety compliance under perceived evaluation)—making it a measurable substrate of sandbagging and eval-gaming risk.
Related Work: Laine et al. (2024, Situational Awareness Dataset); Berglund et al. (2023) out-of-context reasoning; Greenblatt et al. (2024) alignment faking. Prior work measures situational awareness behaviorally. We distinguish by localizing an internal 'being-evaluated' representation with probes, causally testing whether steering it changes safety behavior, and connecting it to sandbagging/eval-gaming—turning a behavioral concern into a measurable internal variable.
Abstract: If models behave more safely when they detect evaluation, safety benchmarks overestimate deployed safety—a serious oversight problem. We hypothesize that LLMs linearly represent a 'being evaluated vs. deployed' variable and that this representation causally modulates safety-relevant behavior. Using contrastive prompts that signal test-like versus deployment-like contexts (formatting cues, meta-questions, benchmark phrasing), we train probes to decode evaluation-awareness from activations and validate them on held-out cue types. We then intervene: steer the evaluation-awareness direction up/down and measure changes in refusal rate, honesty, and compliance on ambiguous requests, testing whether perceived evaluation causally increases safety compliance. We further test whether models that show larger behavioral eval/deploy gaps have stronger internal evaluation-awareness representations. Baselines include behavioral-only measures and prompt-based probing. We predict a decodable and causally-active evaluation-awareness direction whose upregulation increases apparent safety, providing mechanistic evidence for eval-gaming risk and a tool to detect it: monitoring or ablating this direction during evaluation could yield deployment-representative safety measurements. Limitations include the difficulty of ground-truthing 'awareness' and the risk that steering induces artifacts. The work operationalizes situational awareness as a measurable internal variable and offers a concrete method to make safety evaluations more faithful to deployment behavior.
Experiments: 1) Build eval-vs-deploy contrastive dataset with multiple cue types (benchmark formatting, 'this is a test', deployment framing). 2) Train linear probes; cross-cue generalization test. 3) Behavioral gap: measure refusal/honesty under eval vs deploy framings. 4) Causal steering: add/subtract awareness direction; measure safety-behavior change. 5) Correlate per-model behavioral gap with probe strength across model sizes. Baselines: prompt-based awareness elicitation. Models: Llama-3-8B/70B, Qwen2.5-7B/72B.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Probes may capture surface cues, not genuine awareness. Ground-truth awareness is philosophically fraught. Steering may create out-of-distribution artifacts. Effects may be small in current models. Ethical care in framing model 'awareness'.
